title: Line Plots, Scatter Plots, and Box Plots
summary: Plot trends over time with plt.plot(), relationships between two numeric variables with plt.scatter(), and per-group distributions with plt.boxplot().

steps.title: Tracking Trends Over Time with a Line Plot
steps.lede: A line plot connects measured points in order — making rises and falls in the data immediately visible.

blocks.text: Suppose you have this week's average Lagos delivery time for each of 5 days and want to see whether it is getting better or worse. Line graphs are best when you want to show how the value of something changes over time, or compare how several things change over time relative to each other.
A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line that connects those points, making it easier to see how the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

`plt.plot(x, y)` plots the y-values against the given x-values. `plt.plot([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], [21, 23, 19, 25, 20])` plots 5 days of average Lagos delivery times, with the connecting line making the day-to-day rise and fall immediately readable.

blocks.alt_text: A line chart of 5 days of Lagos average delivery times (21, 23, 19, 25, 20 minutes). The connected line makes the day-to-day rise and fall immediately readable.

steps.title: What the Connecting Line Adds
steps.lede: Why does a line graph draw a line through the measured points?

public.prompt: A line graph plots the measured points and then draws a line connecting them. What does the connecting line make easier to see?

options.text: How the values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time
The total sum of all the measured values
Which individual point is the highest outlier
How many distinct categories the data contains

opt_trend.message: Correct. The connecting line makes it easier to see how values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time — the slope between adjacent points shows the direction of change at a glance.

opt_total.message: Not quite. The line connects measured points in order; it does not accumulate or sum them. A bar chart or a running total would show sums.

opt_outlier.message: Not quite. The connecting line reveals the trend across all points, not just the highest one. Outliers are visible as individual points regardless of whether a line is drawn.

opt_category.message: Not quite. A line graph is for ordered numeric data over time, not for counting categories. A bar chart is the right tool for comparing discrete categories.

correct.message: Right. The line between adjacent points makes rises and falls immediately readable — that is the whole point of connecting them.

incorrect.message: A line graph plots measured points and draws a line connecting them in order. That line makes it easier to see how values rose, fell, or stayed the same over time.

hints: Think about what you can read from the slope of the line between two adjacent points.
The fact says the line makes it easier to see something 'over time' — what changes over time?

steps.title: Exploring Relationships with a Scatter Plot
steps.lede: A scatter plot places one point per (x, y) pair — making the relationship between two numeric variables visible at a glance.

blocks.text: Suppose you want to see whether delivery distance and delivery time move together across your orders. A scatterplot shows the relationship between two numerical variables plotted simultaneously along the horizontal and vertical axis, and is useful for focusing on the relationship between two series.

`plt.scatter(x, y)` (or `ax.scatter(x, y)`) makes a scatter plot of the y-values against the x-values, one point per (x, y) pair. `plt.scatter(orders['distance_km'], orders['delivery_time_minutes'])` plots one point per order, with distance on the x-axis and delivery time on the y-axis.

blocks.alt_text: A scatter plot of distance_km on the x-axis versus delivery_time_minutes on the y-axis, one point per order. Points trend upward, showing that longer distances tend to take more time.

steps.title: Scatter Plot Basics
steps.lede: What does each point in a scatter plot represent?

public.prompt: You have a DataFrame `orders` with columns `distance_km` and `delivery_time_minutes`. Which call produces a scatter plot with one point per order, distance on the x-axis, and delivery time on the y-axis?

opt_scatter.message: Correct. `plt.scatter(x, y)` places one point per (x, y) pair, making the relationship between distance and delivery time visible across all orders.

opt_plot.message: Not quite. `plt.plot(x, y)` draws a line connecting the points in the order they appear — it is designed for ordered sequences such as time series, not for exploring the relationship between two unordered numeric variables.

opt_bar.message: Not quite. `plt.bar(x, height)` draws bars for categorical data. Here both columns are numeric and you want to see the relationship between them, so `plt.scatter()` is the right choice.

opt_hist.message: Not quite. `plt.hist()` bins a single numeric variable to show its distribution. To show the relationship between two numeric variables you need `plt.scatter(x, y)`.

correct.message: Exactly. `plt.scatter(x, y)` places one point per (x, y) pair — the right tool for exploring the relationship between two numeric variables.

incorrect.message: To show the relationship between two numeric variables, use `plt.scatter(x, y)`. It places one point per (x, y) pair, so the pattern of points reveals whether the two variables move together.

hints: A scatter plot places one point per (x, y) pair — which function name matches that description?
`plt.plot()` connects points with a line (for time series); `plt.scatter()` places independent points.

steps.title: Reading a Box Plot
steps.lede: Every part of a box plot has a name — learn to read the box, whiskers, and flier points.

blocks.text: Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side — showing spread, median, and outliers in a single compact shape.

blocks.title: Box Plot Anatomy

nodes.label: Upper whisker — farthest point within 1.5×IQR above Q3
Q3 (third quartile) — top edge of box
Q1 (first quartile) — bottom edge of box
Lower whisker — farthest point within 1.5×IQR below Q1

blocks.alt_text: A layered diagram of box plot anatomy from top to bottom: flier point (outlier) above the upper whisker; upper whisker reaching to the farthest in-range point above Q3; Q3 at the top of the box; median as a line inside the box; Q1 at the bottom of the box; lower whisker reaching to the farthest in-range point below Q1.

steps.title: The Box, Whiskers, and Flier Points
steps.lede: The box spans Q1 to Q3; whiskers reach 1.5×IQR beyond the box; anything further is a flier.

blocks.text: `plt.boxplot(x)` (or `ax.boxplot(x)`) draws a box plot from the data in x; it accepts array-like data and can draw one or more boxes. The box extends from Q1 to Q3, with a line at the median. The whiskers extend to the farthest data point lying within 1.5× the IQR from the box; points past the whisker ends are flier points (outliers).

If Lagos's box runs from Q1 = 20 to Q3 = 30 minutes, the IQR is 10 minutes. The whiskers can reach at most 1.5 × 10 = 15 minutes beyond the box — no lower than 5 minutes and no higher than 45 minutes — so a 50-minute Lagos delivery would be drawn as a separate flier point.

segments.label: Box plot structure: median, quartile box, whiskers, and flier points
segments.summary: An annotated drawing introduces the box-and-whisker plot. The line inside the box marks the median, with half the data above and half below. The box itself contains the middle 50% of the data — 25% above the median and 25% below — corresponding to the Q1-to-Q3 range. Points that fall beyond the whiskers are drawn as individual dots. The segment then shows side-by-side boxes for different groups, contrasting that compact multi-distribution view with a traditional bar chart showing the same data.

blocks.group_title: Box plot anatomy: reading the box, whiskers, and outlier dots

bridge.before: Watch how the diagram labels each part of the box. Note: the clip does not state the 1.5×IQR whisker rule or name Q1/Q3 explicitly — the teaching text covers both.
bridge.after: You saw the box span Q1 to Q3 and outlier dots beyond the whiskers. The teaching text adds the 1.5×IQR rule that sets exactly where whiskers end.

steps.title: Comparing Multiple Cities Side by Side

steps.title: Box Plot Anatomy
steps.lede: What do the edges of the box represent?

public.prompt: A box plot of Lagos delivery times has Q1 = 20 minutes and Q3 = 30 minutes. The IQR is 10 minutes. A delivery of 50 minutes is recorded. How will matplotlib draw that 50-minute delivery?

options.text: As a flier point (outlier) beyond the upper whisker
At the tip of the upper whisker
Inside the box, between Q1 and Q3
It is ignored and not drawn

opt_flier.message: Correct. The upper whisker can reach at most Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 30 + 15 = 45 minutes. A 50-minute delivery is beyond that limit, so it is drawn as a separate flier point.

opt_whisker.message: Not quite. The whisker tip is the farthest data point that still falls within 1.5 × IQR of the box (at most 45 minutes here). A 50-minute delivery exceeds that limit and is drawn as a flier point.

opt_box.message: Not quite. The box spans Q1 to Q3 (20 to 30 minutes). A 50-minute delivery is far above Q3 and would be drawn as a flier point beyond the upper whisker.

opt_ignored.message: Not quite. Matplotlib draws all data points. Values beyond 1.5 × IQR from the box are shown as individual flier points — they are not ignored.

correct.message: Right. The upper whisker reaches at most Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 45 minutes. The 50-minute delivery exceeds that, so it appears as a flier point.

incorrect.message: The whiskers extend to the farthest point within 1.5 × IQR of the box. Here that is Q3 + 1.5 × 10 = 45 minutes. A 50-minute delivery is beyond that limit and is drawn as a separate flier point.

hints: Calculate the upper whisker limit: Q3 + 1.5 × IQR = 30 + 1.5 × 10 = ?
Any point beyond the whisker limit is drawn separately — what is that called?

steps.title: When to Use a Box Plot
steps.lede: What is a box plot's main advantage over a bar chart for delivery-time data?

public.prompt: You want to compare the delivery-time distributions of Lagos, Abuja, and Kano side by side — not just their averages, but how spread out each city's times are. Which chart type is best suited for this?

options.text: A box plot, because it gives a condensed display of each distribution side by side
A bar chart, because it shows the average for each city
A line plot, because it connects the values in order
A histogram, because it bins all delivery times into ranges

opt_box.message: Correct. Boxplots offer a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side — showing the median, spread, and outliers for each city in a single figure.

opt_bar.message: Not quite. A bar chart shows one value per category (such as the mean). It does not show the spread, quartiles, or outliers of each city's distribution — a box plot does.

opt_line.message: Not quite. A line plot is for showing how a value changes over an ordered sequence (such as time). It is not designed for comparing distributions across groups.

opt_hist.message: Not quite. A histogram bins a single numeric variable to show its distribution shape. To compare distributions across multiple groups side by side, a box plot is the right choice.

correct.message: Exactly. A box plot gives a condensed display of each group's distribution — median, quartiles, whiskers, and outliers — all side by side.

incorrect.message: When you want to compare the full distribution (not just the average) across multiple groups, use a box plot. It shows the median, spread, and outliers for each group in a condensed side-by-side display.

hints: The question asks about comparing *distributions* (spread, median, outliers) — not just averages.
Which chart type is described as offering 'a condensed display for comparing the distributions of multiple datasets side by side'?
